speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome, I am Dr. Agent. Please describe your symptoms of dizziness, nausea, and imbalance in detail, including when they started and what makes them better or worse. To help narrow this down, have you had any recent head injuries or new medications?

speaker: Patient
text: 27-year-old male. The patient reports a sustained sensation of the room spinning since this morning, which is low grade and constant. He occasionally feels nauseous and has taken diphenhydramine to help him sleep, which also alleviates his symptoms slightly. He mentions recent increased intake of garlic due to trying to recover from a cold a few days ago. Past medical history is unremarkable.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

The description of a sustained, low-grade spinning sensation that improves with diphenhydramine and the lack of recent head trauma or new medications make BPPV less likely than a central cause or vestibular neuritis, but the garlic intake is unlikely to be the direct cause of vertigo. Given the constant nature and improvement with antihistamines, I am concerned about vestibular neuritis or a central lesion. Let me confirm: have you noticed any double vision, slurred speech, weakness in your limbs, or difficulty walking a straight line? REQUEST IMAGES: MRI Brain.
